paragraphs.heading: A book that stirred controversy
paragraphs.edited: Several years ago I was teaching one of my Bible classes when a really important and significant book in the lives of most evangelical Christians came out. It created a firestorm of conversation, waves of controversy, and all kinds of things happening in the Christian world. The book was Love Wins by Rob Bell, and I had all kinds of parents asking me if we were going to read it, or demanding that we don't read it. I had students asking me about it, so I finally said enough is enough — I need to figure out what the story is. So I read it, and I used it as a discussion point for my students.

It's an interesting conversation piece, and something that we ought to talk about.

paragraphs.heading: The Bible is clear
paragraphs.edited: But the Bible is pretty clear. We've talked about the reliability of this text, and Jesus is really clear that hell exists. Yet it's so easy for our students to want to discount that, because we don't necessarily want to be held accountable for our actions, and we don't really want to face the consequences. Who wants to face consequences? So the question I'm often asked is, okay, well, what is hell like? I don't know. It's probably not nice. I don't really know. I don't know if I want to know. It's not God. Hell is the tragic consequence of rejecting God.

paragraphs.heading: Imagining what hell is like
paragraphs.edited: To help your students understand what this tragic consequence would be like, the intro experience takes them through a mini journey of imagining the best possible place — their favorite place. Why do you love it? Describe it. Even put pictures in there. And then remove all of its goodness, everything. Cross out any word that has good meaning. Remove all benefits from that place, all value, all joy, all refreshing qualities, all of it. What would that place be like then? That should help them get into that space of what hell would be like.

paragraphs.edited: I often describe it to students this way. Common grace is the grace that God provides all of us, right? The fact that God is sustaining this world, every breath that I take, the sun that is shining, the air that is blowing, the trees growing, all the rain that falls, all of the things that happen on the righteous and the unrighteous — those are all common grace, because God is here, active and moving in history, and participating in sovereignly taking care of this world.

paragraphs.edited: So then the question comes: well, wait a minute, how come God sends good people to hell? How come God sends anybody to hell? paragraphs.heading: Small group time
paragraphs.edited: So this week, small groups as always — but this week especially is super important, because all that we're talking about is going to come to a bit of a culmination. How can a God who we've already said is good be allowing evil and all those kinds of things, and how can He then have the existence of hell alongside that? If God is so good and so loving and He allows this kind of evil — and this is the question that has been posed to me several times — if God allows evil and allows the suffering to happen, and He's so good, then why would He have hell as a punishment for not believing? It almost seems like there's a contradiction. These are some of the questions that your students may bring up, or some version of them.

paragraphs.heading: Closing encouragement
paragraphs.edited: Well, you made it through this week, and you've almost made it through the rest of the year. We continue to pray for you here, and we continue to pray for your students. I hope that this process of looking at hell and evil and suffering in a very, very real way has helped your students understand not only the point of suffering but the character of God a little bit better — and not only that this points to the existence of God in some sort of philosophical sense, but that even in the midst of suffering God is right there with us, feeling the pain along with us. I hope your students have a better picture of who God is and who Christ is, and what their salvation means, and all of that.
